ABTT fixed (D=10) matches ABTT optimal — no per-layer tuning needed. D=10 is a robust universal default. ABTT alone outperforms ABTT+SIF.

3. “Middle layers — we see this dip” — Density 2x2

“This is baseline, last layer. This is the middle layers, the middle layers we see this dip, that is clear.”

2x2 grid: top row = last layer, bottom = middle layer. Left = baseline (dip visible), right = ABTT (dip corrected).

Architecture effect, not language. mt5-base (no Latin training, 101 languages) achieves 0.987 AUCROC with ABTT (+0.157 over baseline). The dip is a T5-family structural property.

5. “Task B needs redesign” — Duplicate directories problem

“Don't do that. Just take whatever you want to take, lock the sets, run, get numbers. Then repeat with a different seed. We can do maybe five times.”

The problem

For a directory with N files, the old approach created N separate test cases, each removing one file. This produces duplicate near-identical directories during comparison.

The fix (professor's instructions)

Dir sizeRule
1 file (singleton)50% become queries (should match "none"), 50% stay as reference
2 filesTake 1 out as query, keep 1 as reference
3 filesTake 1 out as query, keep 2 as reference
4+ filesTake ~50% out as queries, keep rest as reference

No permutations. Each directory appears exactly once. Lock splits, run, repeat M=5 times with different seeds. Report mean ± std.

Status: DONE. New split implemented in canon_taskb_query_reference_split(). M-seed evaluation ran with 5 seeds across all 6 models.

6. “Token attribution / Integrated gradients” — BERTScore is 2x better

“I found that this new BERTScore is two times better.” — “BERTScore is greedy and this [OT] is optimal?” — “Yes.”

80 example pairs tested across LaBSE, LaTa, PhilTa, Qwen3-0.6B. 6 methods compared:

MethodSparsity ↓Content Focus ↑Shared Token ↑Top-5 Prec ↑
IG + ABTT (baseline)0.410.540.170.54
BERTScore greedy0.080.680.420.59
Optimal Transport (EMD)0.070.560.280.57
Attention cross-sim (Ditto)0.270.330.090.53
DLA0.290.370.110.35
Attention standalone0.350.360.120.51
BERTScore wins. 5x sparser, 2.5x better shared token match, highest content focus. No gradient computation — works on cached embeddings in milliseconds.
Professor wants slightly lower sparsity — “a few predictions, maybe top two will be correct, and human will be happy with that.” Top-K=5 highlighting added.

7. “DLA could be something” — New methods discussed

“Direct Logit Attribution. This method was like specialized method to apply it on the logit of any layer.”

Professor asked about two new methods:

  • Direct Logit Attribution (DLA) — geometric decomposition of per-token contribution. Implemented. Underperformed BERTScore (top-5 precision: 0.35 vs 0.59).
  • Standalone Attention Score — column-mean attention as importance weighting. Implemented. Also underperformed (0.51 vs 0.59).
Conclusion: BERTScore and OT remain the best. DLA and Attention Score are useful reference points but not the primary recommendation for the paper or Leiden demo.

8. “Filtering vs ABTT” — Can you just regex out empty tokens?

Token filtering recovers only 24-47% of baseline-to-ABTT gap. ABTT closes the remaining 53-76%.

LaBSE proof: LaBSE has zero empty tokens. Filtering: +0.02 AUCROC. ABTT: +0.13 AUCROC. Filtering can't explain ABTT's gains.
Token selectivity and importance share (Phase 12c)

89.5% of query-layer pairs show improved selectivity after ABTT.

ABTT unmasks content tokens. LaTa L4 content share: 13.8% → 72.6%.
